- When sentiment is consistently negative (e.g., >50% negative values) and model forecasts remain flat or upward, adjust downward by 3–5% to account for bearish sentiment pressure.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior period), model forecasts often overshoot; reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 5–7 days to avoid overcorrection.
- If official event net supply is negative and bearish sentiment dominates, model should not ignore downward momentum — apply a 2–4% downward bias to 30d forecast mean.
- When sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes (e.g., 3+ consecutive negative sentiment values), model should not assume mean reversion — instead, apply a 1–3% downward adjustment to forecast mean.
- If model forecasts are rising steadily while sentiment is neutral or slightly bullish, check for overconfidence — reduce forecast slope by 10–15% if event context shows net bearish supply.
- For 30d forecasts with high event count and negative supply net, model should not assume “normal” trend — apply a 2–5% downward bias to forecast mean to reflect increased bearish pressure.
- If sentiment history shows a sudden shift from bullish to bearish (e.g., 1–2 negative sentiment spikes), model should not ignore the shift — reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 5–7 days to reflect sentiment reversal.
